tasks.title: bucketBy(N, col) — What It Does at Write Time

description.context: BUCKETING is the second major layout-side optimization beyond partitioning. When you write df.write.bucketBy(N, 'col').sortBy('col').saveAsTable('t'), Spark hashes the column value into N buckets and writes each row to the bucket matching its hash. The number N is chosen by the engineer; common values are 50-500 for production tables. The result on disk is N parquet files (one per bucket), and a 'bucket spec' entry in the table metadata recording the bucket count and column. Bucketing is different from partitioning in two ways. First, bucket files do not produce directories — just files at the table root with predictable names like part-00037-bucketed.parquet. Second, bucketing pre-shuffles data: a downstream query that JOINS or AGGREGATES on the bucketed column can skip the shuffle entirely because matching values are already co-located in matching buckets.
description.task: What did bucketBy(50, 'customer_id') actually do here?

Row Count: 200000

fields.label: What did bucketBy(50, 'customer_id') actually do here?
options: Created 50 directories named bucket=0, bucket=1 etc., each holding one parquet file with the matching customer_ids. The bucket count is encoded in directory names.

Hashed every row's customer_id into one of 50 buckets and wrote each bucket's rows into one parquet file at the table root. The bucket spec was registered in the catalog so downstream queries can use it.
Sorted the entire table by customer_id and wrote 50 evenly-sized parquet files in customer_id order. The 50 number determines file count only; bucketing is just a synonym for repartition + sort.
Created a hash index on customer_id stored in a separate index file alongside the parquet files. The 50 indicates the index granularity (50 hash buckets per index level).
fields.correctAnswer: Hashed every row's customer_id into one of 50 buckets and wrote each bucket's rows into one parquet file at the table root. The bucket spec was registered in the catalog so downstream queries can use it.
fields.rationale: Hash distribution and catalog metadata are the two essential elements at write time.Files appear at the table root, named like part-00000-bucketed...
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats bucketing as creating directories; it creates files at the root level.

tasks.pssReference: PSI2 lesson 6 (Bucketing — write semantics), PSI3 lesson 5 (Bucketing for Shuffle Skip).

tasks.title: Bucketing vs Partitioning

description.context: Bucketing and partitioning solve different problems. Partitioning enables PRUNING — Spark skips entire directories that don't match a filter. Bucketing enables SHUFFLE SKIP — Spark recognizes pre-distributed data and avoids re-shuffling for joins/aggregations on the bucketed column. The cardinality requirements differ too. Partition columns need 10-10,000 distinct values (each becomes a directory). Bucket columns can have any cardinality — bucketBy(50, 'customer_id') with 200K customers works fine because all 200K values hash into just 50 buckets. The choice is not exclusive: a table can be BOTH partitioned (e.g., by date) AND bucketed (by customer_id) at the same time.
description.task: What is the structural difference and which optimization does each enable?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Code A: customer_dim.write.partitionBy('region').parquet('layout_a/')

Code B: customer_dim.write.bucketBy(50, 'customer_id').sortBy('customer_id').saveAsTable('layout_b')

Schema: customer_id (200K distinct), region (4 distinct), customer_type, daily_kw

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Same customer_dim written two ways — once as partitionBy('region'), once as bucketBy(50, 'customer_id') — visible side-by-side

fields.label: What is the structural difference and which optimization does each enable?
options: Layout A is the production-grade layout; Layout B's flat file structure indicates a write failure. Spark normally creates partitioned output by default, so a bucket-only output without any partition columns is rarely correct.

Layout A is the production-grade layout; Layout B's flat file structure indicates a write failure. Spark normally creates partitioned output by default; bucket-only output without partition columns is rarely correct.

Layout A enables partition pruning on region (skip non-matching directories). Layout B enables shuffle-skip on customer_id joins (matching customer_ids land in matching buckets). Different layouts solve different problems.
Layout A and Layout B are mutually exclusive — a table cannot be both partitioned and bucketed at the same time. Combining requires Delta Lake; standard parquet supports one or the other only.
fields.correctAnswer: Layout A enables partition pruning on region (skip non-matching directories). Layout B enables shuffle-skip on customer_id joins (matching customer_ids land in matching buckets). Different layouts solve different problems.
fields.rationale: The two layouts target different optimizations.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats the structural difference as cosmetic; it directly drives different optimizations.

tasks.pssReference: PSI2 lessons 5-6 (Partitioning vs Bucketing — semantic differences).

tasks.title: BucketedTableScan in the Plan

description.context: When you query a bucketed table and Spark recognizes the bucket spec, the plan changes shape. Look for two signals. First, the FileScan operator becomes a BUCKETED FileScan or shows 'SelectedBucketsCount: M out of N' — proving Spark used the bucket layout. Second, when joining a bucketed table to another table on the bucketed column, the Exchange that would normally appear above the bucketed side DISAPPEARS — Spark trusts that data is already pre-distributed by the hash. The other side may still need a shuffle (unless it's also bucketed compatibly), but eliminating one side of the shuffle is significant savings.
description.task: What does this plan tell you about whether bucketing helped?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Left Table: positions (12M rows, NOT bucketed)

Right Table: customer_dim_bucketed (200K rows, bucketBy(50, 'customer_id'))

Join Key: customer_id

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Plan from a NordGrid join between a bucketed customer_dim and a non-bucketed positions table — bucket spec engages on one side

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
# Query: positions.join(customer_dim_bucketed, on='customer_id', how='inner')

== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- ShuffledHashJoin [customer_id#0], [customer_id#50], Inner, BuildRight
   :- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id#0, 50)
   :  +- FileScan parquet positions [customer_id#0, daily_kw#3, region#5]
   +- FileScan parquet customer_dim_bucketed [customer_id#50, customer_type#52]
      SelectedBucketsCount: 50 out of 50
      Bucketed: true
      ⟵ NO Exchange operator above this scan

# Compare with same join if customer_dim were NOT bucketed:
#   +- Sort [customer_id ASC]
#      +- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id, 200)   ← extra shuffle
#         +- FileScan parquet customer_dim_unbucketed

fields.label: What does this plan tell you about whether bucketing helped?
options: Bucketing did not help — the Exchange on the positions side proves a shuffle still happened. Bucket-aware optimization only fires when BOTH sides are bucketed compatibly. Useless effort to bucket only customer_dim.

Bucketing engaged on customer_dim_bucketed (Bucketed: true, no Exchange above). The other side (positions) still needed a shuffle. The non-bucketed side's shuffle uses 50 partitions to match the bucket count — clean handoff. One shuffle eliminated of two.

The plan is misleading — Bucketed: true is informational only. The actual runtime behavior shuffles both sides regardless of what the plan operator says. Bucketing benefits only appear if you set spark.sql.bucketing.enabled=true, which is off by default in Spark 3.5+.

Bucketing engaged on both sides. The positions side appears to have an Exchange but that's actually a fast bucket-rehash done locally, not a true cross-cluster shuffle. Both reads are bucketed; both shuffles are eliminated.
fields.correctAnswer: Bucketing engaged on customer_dim_bucketed (Bucketed: true, no Exchange above). The other side (positions) still needed a shuffle. The non-bucketed side's shuffle uses 50 partitions to match the bucket count — clean handoff. One shuffle eliminated of two.
fields.rationale: The plan signals are independent of metadata claims; runtime evidence determines whether the bucket spec is honored.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats bucketing as all-or-nothing; one-sided bucketing still eliminates one shuffle.
Option C: Invents a disable-by-default flag.5+.

tasks.pssReference: PSI3 lesson 5 (Bucketing for Shuffle Skip — single-side and double-side patterns).

tasks.title: Bucket Count Mismatch — Why Bucketing Did Not Help

description.context: Bucket-side shuffle skip only works when bucket counts MATCH between the two tables being joined. If table A has 50 buckets and table B has 200 buckets on the same column, Spark CANNOT skip the shuffle on either side — the hash distributions don't align (a customer_id that hashes to bucket 7 of 50 ends up in bucket 28 of 200, and Spark cannot pair them without redistributing). The plan signal: Exchange operators appear above BOTH bucketed sides, both shuffling to 200 partitions (or some other unified count). The bucket counts are visible in catalog metadata; mismatches are silent — Spark does not warn.
description.task: Why did bucketing fail to eliminate the shuffles, and what is the fix?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Left Table: positions_bucketed (bucketBy(50, 'customer_id'))

Right Table: customer_dim_bucketed (bucketBy(200, 'customer_id'))

Engineer Assumption: both bucketed → no shuffle

Actual Observation: both sides shuffle, same as if neither were bucketed

Performance Vs Unbucketed: identical (no benefit observed)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Two bucketed tables joined together but with mismatched bucket counts (50 vs 200), so neither side benefits

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
# Catalog metadata
DESCRIBE EXTENDED positions_bucketed:
  Num Buckets: 50
  Bucket Columns: [customer_id]

DESCRIBE EXTENDED customer_dim_bucketed:
  Num Buckets: 200
  Bucket Columns: [customer_id]

# Plan for: positions_bucketed.join(customer_dim_bucketed, on='customer_id')

+- SortMergeJoin [customer_id], [customer_id], Inner
   :- Sort [customer_id ASC]
   :  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id, 200)   ← left shuffles
   :     +- FileScan parquet positions_bucketed
   +- Sort [customer_id ASC]
      +- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id, 200)   ← right shuffles
         +- FileScan parquet customer_dim_bucketed

fields.label: Why did bucketing fail to eliminate the shuffles, and what is the fix?
options: Bucketing only works for inner joins; the optimizer disabled bucket-skip because of the implicit isnotnull condition added by Spark for safety. Fix: explicitly cast customer_id to NOT NULL via dropna() before the join is invoked.

Bucketing only works for inner joins; the optimizer disabled bucket-skip because of the implicit isnotnull condition added by Spark for safety. Fix: explicitly cast customer_id to NOT NULL via dropna() before the join.

Both tables ARE benefiting from bucketing internally; the visible Exchanges are pre-bucketing rehash steps that Spark adds for safety. The actual shuffle volume is much smaller than the plan suggests. Fix: nothing needed.

The bucket counts (50 vs 200) don't match. Spark cannot align hash distributions across mismatched bucket counts; both sides must shuffle. Fix: rewrite both tables with the SAME bucket count (e.g., both 200) so the bucket spec aligns.
fields.correctAnswer: The bucket counts (50 vs 200) don't match. Spark cannot align hash distributions across mismatched bucket counts; both sides must shuffle. Fix: rewrite both tables with the SAME bucket count (e.g., both 200) so the bucket spec aligns.
fields.rationale: Bucket-aware shuffle skip requires identical bucket counts on the join column.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Invents a type-mismatch issue not implied by the scenario.
Option B: Invents an inner-only or null-safety constraint.

tasks.pssReference: PSI3 lesson 5 (Bucketing — bucket count alignment requirements).

tasks.title: OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY — Reading the Delta Log

description.context: Z-ORDERING is a Delta Lake feature that physically reorganizes file layout to co-locate rows with similar values across MULTIPLE columns. It is invoked via OPTIMIZE table ZORDER BY (col1, col2). The Z-order is a multi-dimensional space-filling curve: rows whose (col1, col2) values are close in the 2D space end up in the same parquet file. After Z-ordering, every parquet file gets min/max statistics for the Z-ordered columns; queries with range filters on those columns can SKIP files entirely. Z-order is what enables file-skipping on multi-column filters that simple partitioning cannot provide. It only works on Delta tables (not plain parquet) because it needs the transaction log to record the optimization.
description.task: What did OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY (region, date) do, and what does it enable?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Code: spark.sql("OPTIMIZE silver.meters ZORDER BY (region, date)")

Table Size Before: 12 GB across 800 parquet files

Table Size After: 12 GB across 800 parquet files (rewritten, not recompressed)

Operation Duration: 4 minutes

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Delta transaction log entry showing OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY (region, date) operation and resulting per-file statistics

evidence.label: Snippet

fields.label: What did OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY (region, date) do, and what does it enable?
options: OPTIMIZE merged 800 small files into fewer large ones; ZORDER BY is just an alphabetization marker that has no runtime effect. The transaction log entry records the operation for time-travel only.

ZORDER physically reorganized files so rows with similar (region, date) values are co-located in the same parquet file. Per-file min/max statistics now allow Spark to skip files whose range cannot match a query's (region, date) filter.
OPTIMIZE created Z-order indexes alongside the parquet files; the indexes are read at query time to filter rows. Without ZORDER indexes, queries fall back to full-table scans on Delta tables.

ZORDER changed the table's primary key to (region, date). Future updates must use these columns; reads not filtering on (region, date) will fail with a key-mismatch error from the transaction log validator.
fields.correctAnswer: ZORDER physically reorganized files so rows with similar (region, date) values are co-located in the same parquet file. Per-file min/max statistics now allow Spark to skip files whose range cannot match a query's (region, date) filter.
fields.rationale: Multi-dimensional clustering plus per-file statistics together create the file-skipping foundation.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats ZORDER as cosmetic; it physically reorganizes data.

tasks.pssReference: PSI2 lesson 7 (Delta Z-Ordering — semantics and the transaction log).

tasks.title: Z-Order Skipped Files — How to Read the Stats

description.context: After ZORDER, the proof that Z-order helped is in the FILE-SKIPPING METRIC. When you run a query against a Z-ordered Delta table and look at the plan or the Spark UI, you see a metric called numFilesRead vs numFilesTotal. If numFilesRead is much less than numFilesTotal, file-skipping engaged — Spark used the per-file min/max stats to rule out files that cannot match the filter. The metric is dollar-of-truth proof that Z-order is paying off; without it, you have no idea whether OPTIMIZE actually helped. A fully effective Z-order produces numFilesRead values 10-100× smaller than numFilesTotal for typical filtered queries.
description.task: What does numFilesRead: 12 out of 800 tell you?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Code: spark.read.format('delta').load('silver.meters').filter((col('region') == 'NORTH') & (col('date').between('2025-04-20', '2025-04-25'))).count()

Table Z Ordered By: (region, date)

Total Files: 800

Files Actually Read: 12

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Plan from a query against the Z-ordered NordGrid silver.meters table showing numFilesRead vs numFilesTotal

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
# Plan output (Delta Lake metrics visible)

+- HashAggregate(keys=[], functions=[count(1)])
   +- FileScan parquet silver.meters [region, date, daily_kw]
      DataFilters: [(region = NORTH), (date >= 2025-04-20), (date <= 2025-04-25)]
      ReadSchema: struct<region:string, date:date, ...>
      
      Delta scan metrics:
        numFilesTotal:    800
        numFilesRead:      12
        bytesRead:        ~180 MB (out of 12 GB total)
        filesSkippedByDataSkipping: 788

# Comparison: same query on a NON-Z-ordered version of the table
#   numFilesTotal:    800
#   numFilesRead:     800   ← every file opened
#   bytesRead:        ~12 GB
#   No file-skipping; full scan with row-level filter post-read

fields.label: What does numFilesRead: 12 out of 800 tell you?
options: Z-order reduced the file count from 800 to 12 during OPTIMIZE; the table now physically has only 12 files. numFilesTotal still says 800 because that count is cached from before OPTIMIZE. Refresh metadata to update.

Z-order randomly sampled 12 of 800 files for an approximate count; the result is statistical, not exact. To get exact counts on Z-ordered tables, set spark.sql.zorder.exactCount=true to disable sampling.
12 files is the bucketing output (50/4 ≈ 12 buckets matching the filter); the table was bucketed not Z-ordered. The 'numFilesRead' metric is misnamed; it actually counts buckets read at scan time.

Z-order skipped 788 files because their per-file min/max stats ruled them out for the (region, date) range filter. Only 12 files had stats overlapping the query range; Spark read those and applied the filter at row level.
fields.correctAnswer: Z-order skipped 788 files because their per-file min/max stats ruled them out for the (region, date) range filter. Only 12 files had stats overlapping the query range; Spark read those and applied the filter at row level.
fields.rationale: Z-order's payoff is file-skipping at query time.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats OPTIMIZE as compacting to 12 files; it rewrites all 800 files clustered by Z-order.

tasks.pssReference: PSI2 lesson 7 (Delta Z-Ordering — file-skipping mechanics and metrics).

description.context: Z-order only helps queries that filter on the Z-ordered columns. If the engineer ran OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY (customer_id) but their queries filter on (region, date), the Z-order does NOTHING — there are no min/max stats on (region, date) to enable file-skipping. The plan's diagnostic: numFilesRead == numFilesTotal, even though OPTIMIZE was run recently and the team thinks Z-order is helping. This is a recognition failure mode common in Mid-level pipelines: someone runs OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY against the wrong column because they don't know which queries will hit the table later, or because they Z-ordered against an old query pattern that has since changed.
description.task: Why is file-skipping not engaging despite a recent OPTIMIZE, and what is the fix?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:

Table Z Ordered By: (customer_id) — wrong column

Actual Query Filter: (region, date) — different columns

Last Optimize Run: this morning

Team Assumption: Z-order is helping

Actual Observation: numFilesRead == numFilesTotal — full scan

evidence.content: Plan showing a Z-ordered Delta table queried on a different column than the Z-order column — file-skipping fails to engage

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
# Catalog metadata
DESCRIBE EXTENDED silver.meters
  Format: delta
  Last OPTIMIZE: 2025-05-04 03:14 (3 hours ago)
  Z-Order columns: [customer_id]
  Statistics: customer_id min/max stats per file

# Plan for: filter((region == 'NORTH') & (date BETWEEN '2025-04-20' AND '2025-04-25'))

+- HashAggregate(keys=[], functions=[count(1)])
   +- FileScan delta silver.meters
      DataFilters: [(region = NORTH), (date >= 2025-04-20), (date <= 2025-04-25)]
      
      Delta scan metrics:
        numFilesTotal:    800

fields.label: Why is file-skipping not engaging despite a recent OPTIMIZE, and what is the fix?
options: OPTIMIZE was run against the table but Z-order skipping requires query rewrite; the engineer must add a hint /*+ DATA_SKIPPING */ to enable it. Fix: add the hint to all queries against this table.

Z-order columns and query filter columns don't match. Z-order on customer_id provides min/max stats on customer_id — useless for queries filtering region/date. Fix: re-run OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY (region, date) to match actual query patterns.
OPTIMIZE was too recent (3 hours); Z-order takes ~24 hours to propagate stats through the transaction log to the query planner. Fix: wait for stats propagation OR run REFRESH TABLE silver.meters.

Z-order requires bucketing first; the table is Z-ordered without being bucketed, which Spark silently treats as a no-op. Fix: rewrite the table with bucketBy(50, 'customer_id') BEFORE running OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY.
fields.correctAnswer: Z-order columns and query filter columns don't match. Z-order on customer_id provides min/max stats on customer_id — useless for queries filtering region/date. Fix: re-run OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY (region, date) to match actual query patterns.
fields.rationale: Statistics generated by OPTIMIZE only cover the columns named in the ZORDER BY clause.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Invents a hint requirement; Delta data-skipping is automatic when stats exist.

tasks.title: Bucketing Without OPTIMIZE — Stale File Layout

description.context: Bucketing is a WRITE-TIME optimization, but it can drift over time. A bucketed table that is appended to (not rewritten) accumulates new files that are NOT bucket-aligned with the original layout. After enough appends, the table effectively has 'old buckets + new chunks' — and Spark's query optimizer cannot use the bucket spec for shuffle skip because not all files conform to it. The diagnostic signal: BucketedTableScan in the plan but with SelectedBucketsCount: 0 out of 50 (or some other partial number), AND Exchange operators reappearing on the bucketed side. The fix is to rewrite the table periodically — INSERT OVERWRITE bucketed table SELECT * FROM bucketed table — to re-apply the bucket layout to all data.
description.task: Why did Spark refuse to use the bucket spec, and what is the fix?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Table: positions_bucketed (bucketBy(50, 'customer_id'), originally written 3 weeks ago)

Append Pattern: daily INSERT INTO without OVERWRITE

Current State: 50 original bucket files + 21 daily append files (no bucket alignment)

Engineer Assumption: bucketing still works because metadata says 50 buckets

Actual Observation: Exchange reappeared on the bucketed side

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Plan against a bucketed table that has had 3 weeks of daily appends without rewrite — bucketing has drifted, shuffle reappears

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
# Catalog metadata (still records the bucket spec)
DESCRIBE EXTENDED positions_bucketed
  Num Buckets: 50
  Bucket Columns: [customer_id]

# Actual file layout
$ ls /warehouse/positions_bucketed/
  part-00000-bucketed-c000.parquet  (3.6 MB)   ← original 50 bucket files
  part-00001-bucketed-c000.parquet
  ...
  part-00049-bucketed-c000.parquet
  part-00000-append-2025-04-14.parquet  ← 21 daily appends (NOT bucket-aligned)
  part-00000-append-2025-04-15.parquet
  ...
  part-00000-append-2025-05-04.parquet

# Plan for: positions_bucketed.join(customer_dim_bucketed_50, on='customer_id')

+- SortMergeJoin [customer_id], [customer_id], Inner
   :- Sort [customer_id ASC]
   :  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id, 50)   ← REAPPEARED!
   :     +- FileScan parquet positions_bucketed
   :        SelectedBucketsCount: 0 out of 50
   :        Bucketed: false   ← Spark refused to honor the bucket spec
   +- (other side, normally bucketed)

fields.label: Why did Spark refuse to use the bucket spec, and what is the fix?
options: The 21 daily append files are not bucket-aligned (they were written without bucketBy). Spark sees the mixed layout and refuses to honor the bucket spec. Fix: INSERT OVERWRITE the table to rewrite all files with bucket alignment.

The Exchange is a misreading of the plan; it's actually a no-op operator that AQE inserts and removes at runtime. SelectedBucketsCount: 0 means 'all 50 selected without filter' (not 'zero selected'). Fix: nothing — bucketing is working.

DELTA tables don't support bucketing; this is a Delta table that lost its bucket metadata during the last transaction log compaction. Fix: convert the table back to plain parquet to restore bucket support.

Catalyst auto-disabled bucketing for tables over 1 month old; Spark prevents stale bucket layouts from misleading the optimizer. Fix: ALTER TABLE ... SET TBLPROPERTIES ('spark.bucket.refresh'='true') to re-enable.
fields.correctAnswer: The 21 daily append files are not bucket-aligned (they were written without bucketBy). Spark sees the mixed layout and refuses to honor the bucket spec. Fix: INSERT OVERWRITE the table to rewrite all files with bucket alignment.
fields.rationale: Bucketing's correctness depends on every file conforming to the bucket layout.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Misreads SelectedBucketsCount: 0; that explicitly means zero buckets used.
Option C: Conflates bucketing with Delta.

tasks.pssReference: PSI2 lesson 6 (Bucketing — append-time drift and refresh requirements).

tasks.title: Audit a Mid-Layout Pipeline

description.context: A NordGrid Mid engineer claims they layout-tuned a daily-billing pipeline with partitioning, bucketing, AND Z-ordering. They show the senior the table layouts AND the resulting plan and ask for review. The senior asks the engineer to verify EACH layout decision by reading the plan — not by trusting the metadata. Five sub-questions audit five different layout claims.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: 50-line layout-aware NordGrid pipeline; verify each layout intervention against the plan

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
# Layout setup (NordGrid silver layer)

# Table: silver.meters
#   Format: delta
#   partitionBy: (date)              ← 30 daily partitions for April 2025
#   Z-Order:    (region, customer_type)
#   Last OPTIMIZE: 2025-05-04 02:00 (today, 4 hours ago)

# Table: silver.customer_dim_bucketed
#   Format: parquet
#   bucketBy(50, 'customer_id') sortBy('customer_id')

# Pipeline code
result = (spark.read.format('delta').load('silver.meters')
    .filter((col('date').between('2025-04-01', '2025-04-30')) & (col('region') == 'NORTH'))
    .join(spark.table('silver.customer_dim_bucketed'), on='customer_id', how='inner')
    .groupBy('customer_type')
    .agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total_kw')))
result.collect()
result.explain()

# Plan output (post-execution)
+- HashAggregate(keys=[customer_type], functions=[sum(daily_kw)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_type, 50)
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[customer_type], functions=[partial_sum(daily_kw)])
         +- Project [customer_type, daily_kw]
            +- ShuffledHashJoin [customer_id], [customer_id], Inner, BuildRight
               :- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id, 50)
               :  +- FileScan delta silver.meters
               :     PartitionFilters: [(date >= 2025-04-01), (date <= 2025-04-30)]
               :     PartitionCount: 30
               :     numFilesTotal: 240, numFilesRead: 60, filesSkippedByDataSkipping: 180
               +- FileScan parquet silver.customer_dim_bucketed
                  SelectedBucketsCount: 50 out of 50
                  Bucketed: true

tasks.title: Five Missed Layout Opportunities

description.context: Final SLI exercise. A NordGrid pipeline runs correctly but is suboptimal at the layout level. The senior asks the engineer to read the layout AND the plan and identify FIVE missed layout opportunities. Each one is a different category: missed partition pruning, wrong bucket column, missing Z-order on hot column, small-file aggregation needed, OPTIMIZE not scheduled. The plan tells the story; the table layouts look fine on their own but together miss several wins.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: 55-line NordGrid pipeline with 5 embedded missed layout-level opportunities

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
# Layout setup

# Table: bronze.events_log (parquet, NOT partitioned, NOT bucketed)
